\subsection{Stage 1: every configuration for 200 million steps}
\label{sec:pixel-montezuma-fll-stage-1}

Stage 1 runs every configuration of the fast last layer and of RND (\Cref{tab:pixel-montezuma-fll-swept}), eight
seeds each, so that each side's best configuration can be chosen by its mean score over the run. On PointMaze
Large the fast last layer at step $0.1$ reached the goal at about half of RND's mean capped first-goal time
(\Cref{tab:beat-rnd-discovery-arrival,tab:beat-rnd-discovery-step-cost}); no hyperparameter had been swept on this
game before.

\paragraph{The method.} Define $f(x)$ as the frozen random target's $512$ outputs for the frame $x$ (the newest
frame of the next observation, normalized as in RND), $\phi(x)$ as the predictor's last hidden features with a
constant $1$ appended ($513$ entries), and $V$ as the predictor's last dense layer ($513\times512$, its bias in the
last row). RND's bonus of a transition is then $\tfrac12\lVert V^{\top}\phi(x) - f(x)\rVert^2$. Define $N = 128$ as
the environments of one policy, $G$ as the sharing group and $\eta \in (0, 1)$ as the step size. The $N$
environments form $N/G$ fixed groups of $G$ consecutive environments, and group $j$ has its own temporary layer
$\tilde V_j$, set to $V$ at the start of every rollout. At rollout step $t$, define $\Phi_{tj}$ as the $G$ rows
$\phi(x)^{\top}$ of the group's next frames, $E_{tj}$ as the $G$ rows of their errors
$\tilde V_j^{\top}\phi(x) - f(x)$, and $\Phi_{tj}^{+}$ as the pseudo-inverse of $\Phi_{tj}$, computed in 64-bit
floating point from rows scaled to unit length with a ridge of $10^{-9}$. Each transition's bonus is
$\tfrac12\lVert \tilde V_j^{\top}\phi(x) - f(x)\rVert^2$, read before the layer changes; then the layer takes the
change with the smallest sum of squared entries that multiplies each of the $G$ errors by $1 - \eta$:
\begin{equation}
\tilde V_j \leftarrow \tilde V_j - \eta\,\Phi_{tj}^{+}E_{tj}.
\end{equation}
A frame met again later in the same rollout, by any environment of the group, therefore pays less. The temporary
layers are dropped after the rollout; the predictor itself trains only in PPO's epochs, as in RND, and the bonuses
go through RND's discounted sum and running divisor unchanged. With $\eta = 0$ the trainer is the archived
baseline's, which was checked against that baseline's records before the stage. Every run has $128$ environments
per policy, RND's included: the sharing group only splits them for the bonus (one group of $128$, $8$ groups of
$16$ or $32$ groups of $4$), and PPO's batch, its updates and the predictor's training are the same for all three.

\paragraph{How to read the measures.} Define $K$ as the number of policies (seeds) of a configuration and $B$ as
the budget in agent steps per policy ($200$ million in stage 1). A window is $61$ consecutive updates, $999{,}424$
agent steps of one policy, and $m$ is the number of whole windows in $B$ ($200$ in stage 1). Define $g_{ik}$ as the
number of training games of policy $i$ that finished in window $k$ and $s_{ik}$ as the sum of their scores per game
(\Cref{tab:pixel-montezuma-fll-game}). The window value is $v_{ik} = s_{ik}/g_{ik}$, or $v_{i,k-1}$ when no game
finished in window $k$ ($v_{i0} = 0$).
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item \textbf{Mean score over the run} (chooses each side's configuration) and the final level beside it, which
breaks ties:
\begin{equation}
S(B) = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\frac{1}{m}\sum_{k=1}^{m}v_{ik},
\qquad
S_{\text{last}}(B) = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\frac{10}{m}\sum_{k=0.9m+1}^{m}v_{ik}.
\end{equation}
\item \textbf{First-time step of an event.} For an event in update $u$ (counted from $1$) at rollout step $t$
(counted from $0$), $T = (u-1)\times16{,}384 + (t+1)\times128$: the policy's training steps when it happened, exact
to one step of its $128$ environments. Events of the $50$ random warm-up rollouts are not counted. Every run
records it for the first key, the first door, the first exit from the start room and the room it led to, every
room, every item type and the first enemy killed.
\item \textbf{Mean capped first exit from the start room.} Define $T_i$ as the first-time step of policy $i$'s
first exit ($T_i = \infty$ if it never leaves). Then $E(B) = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\min(T_i, B)$; smaller is
better, and ties go to the larger share of policies that left.
\item \textbf{Rooms reached:} the number of the $24$ rooms a policy has been in at least once by $B$.
\end{enumerate}
In stages 2 and 3 the method counts as ahead of RND when, on seeds that chose neither configuration, the $95\%$
interval over seeds of the difference in $S(B)$ (method minus RND) lies entirely above zero and that of the
difference in $S_{\text{last}}(B)$ does not lie entirely below zero; the intervals resample seeds, never games or
windows.

\paragraph{Stage-1 results.} Stage 1 is complete: all \PixelFllRunsFinished{} of its \PixelFllRunsPlanned{} runs
trained their $200$ million steps, so all $8$ seeds of every configuration are at the budget (records read at
\PixelFllReadAt{}; \Cref{tab:pixel-montezuma-fll-status}).
\Cref{tab:pixel-montezuma-fll-score-rnd,tab:pixel-montezuma-fll-score-group-128,tab:pixel-montezuma-fll-score-group-16,tab:pixel-montezuma-fll-score-group-4}
give $S(B)$ over the $8$ seeds with its standard error (the sample standard deviation over the seeds divided by
$\sqrt{8}$) and $S_{\text{last}}(B)$; they choose the configurations of stage 2. No run was stopped, held or
chosen on the early numbers while stage 1 trained.
$E(B)$ is tabulated with the full seeds.

The first-time-step tables give, for each configuration, the first key, the first door and the first exit
from the start room. Each such cell holds the median first-time step $T$ over the configuration's $8$ seeds, in
million steps, where a seed that has not had the event counts as later than every seed that has; ``not yet'' means
the median seed did not have it within the $200$ million steps every seed trained (the column ``steps trained''),
and beside the value $k/n$ counts the $k$ seeds that had it of the $n$ trained. The last row of every first-time-step table is the archived baseline: the final
training of \Cref{sec:pixel-montezuma-final-training}, RND at weight $1$ with the same trainer on seeds $1$ to
$12$ for $2$ billion steps. It was recorded before the game events existed, so its first key and first exit are
known only to the end of their update and its first door is not recorded. Every run of
\PixelFllWarmUpKeySeeds{} opened a door and left the start room in its first update, before its first counted key: one
of its $128$ environments picked up the key during the random warm-up rollouts, whose events are not counted, and
carried it into training. The first update is the same in every configuration of a seed (the policy has not been
trained, and the warm-up actions depend on the seed only), so that seed's first door and first exit are equal in
every configuration and add nothing to their comparison.

\paragraph{Findings of stage 1.}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=*]
\item \textbf{Exits from the start room.} \PixelFllRndLeft{} of the \PixelFllRndStarted{} RND runs and
\PixelFllFastLeft{} of the \PixelFllFastStarted{} fast-last-layer runs left the start room within the budget. All
\PixelFllArchivedLeft{} archived runs left it, at a median of \PixelFllArchivedExit{} million steps.
\item \textbf{A door without an exit.} \PixelFllFastDoorNoExit{} fast-last-layer runs and \PixelFllRndDoorNoExit{}
RND runs opened a door but did not leave the start room within the budget.
\item \textbf{Standing checks} (\Cref{tab:pixel-montezuma-fll-checks}): \PixelFllLockedExits{} exits with both
doors locked, \PixelFllExitBeforeKey{} runs whose first exit came before their first counted key with no door
opened before it, and \PixelFllNonFinite{} values that are not finite.
\item \textbf{A key from the warm-up.} \PixelFllWarmUpKeyRuns{} runs, all of \PixelFllWarmUpKeySeeds{}, left
the start room in their first update with a key picked up during the random warm-up rollouts; their first door and
first exit are those of the random warm-up, not of training.
\item \textbf{The choice for stage 2}
(\Cref{tab:pixel-montezuma-fll-score-rnd,tab:pixel-montezuma-fll-score-group-16,tab:pixel-montezuma-fll-score-group-4}).
The method's best configuration by $S(B)$ is sharing group $4$, step size $0.01$, weight $1$
($1{,}889 \pm 278$). Its runner-up, sharing group $16$, step size $0.01$, weight $2$ ($1{,}779 \pm 326$), lies
within one standard error of it, so both go to stage 2. RND's best is weight $2$ ($1{,}379 \pm 209$). Since RND's
best weight is not the archived baseline's weight $1$, RND is trained again at weight $2$ in stage 2 instead of
reusing the archived runs.
\item \textbf{No claim yet.} On seeds $13$ to $20$ the method's best is ahead of RND's best by about $510$, but each
of the method's two picks is the best of $72$ configurations and RND's the best of $6$, and a pick looks better on
the seeds that chose it than on new seeds. RND at weight $1$ scored $1{,}277 \pm 223$ on seeds $13$ to $20$ against
$1{,}702 \pm 203$ for the archived baseline's seeds $1$ to $12$ at the same weight, so the block of seeds alone moves
$S(B)$ by hundreds. The comparison is made in stage 2, on seeds $1$ to $12$, which chose nothing.
\item \textbf{What one seed cannot show.} The archived baseline's twelve seeds, all of one configuration, first left
the start room between \PixelFllArchivedExitFirst{} and \PixelFllArchivedExitLast{} million steps, so the value of
a single seed does not rank configurations.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Stage 2: the chosen configurations on seeds that chose nothing}

Stage 2 trains three configurations on seeds $1$ to $12$ for $1$ billion steps each ($36$ runs), with the
learning-rate schedule at its $2$-billion-step horizon as in stage 1, so stage 3 continues the winner and RND to
$2$ billion steps:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=*]
\item the fast last layer, sharing group $4$, step size $0.01$, weight $1$ (the method's best in stage 1);
\item the fast last layer, sharing group $16$, step size $0.01$, weight $2$ (its runner-up, within one standard
error);
\item RND at weight $2$ (RND's best in stage 1).
\end{enumerate}
Each of the method's configurations is compared with RND by the rule of the previous subsection, paired by seed.
